newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Grain-Markets brace for pool price cut.
newsitem.headline: Australian Grain-Markets brace for pool price cut.

text.p: The Australian grain industry is expecting the Australian Wheat Board (AWB) to cut its pool prices for exported wheat by A$5.00 to A$10.00 a tonne in its regular revision this week.

Estimated pool prices to be paid to producers by the AWB, Australia's statutory authority monopoly exporter, presently stand at A$200.00 a tonne for 1996/97 benchmark grade Australian Standard White (ASW) and at A$190.00-A$200.00 for 1997/98 wheat.
A pools price cut would follow falling prices in Chicago, not mirrored in Australian markets which are partly propped up by pools prices.

A pools price cut of A$5.00-A$10.00 could bring wheat futures back to the A$165.00-A$168.00 area, broker Phil Lindsay of Ord Minnett Jardine Fleming Futures said on Friday. Futures market leader January 1998 closed on Friday at A$172.50.
The expected pools price cut was the most important bear point in a mixed bag in Australian grains markets last week.

It formed a counterweight to the strongest bull factor, a forecast by Australia's weather bureau that large areas of eastern Australia were likely to be significantly drier than normal in the southern hemisphere winter and spring.
The forecast was based on current El Nino sea temperature and Southern Oscillation Index air pressure readings.
"The dominant factor this week is the theory of the El Nino. The weather bureau has been scaring the hell out of everyone with threats of drought," Ord Minnett's Lindsay said.
The weather bureau report was a wild card prompting many to hedge by purchasing at current levels, he said.
On balance, Lindsay now sees Australia shaping up for an average wheat year in 1997/98. "It depends on how the follow-up rains occur. It could go either way," he said.
Sporadic rain fell in New South Wales toward the end of last week, but Victoria still needs rain to complete sowing, while South Australia is in patchy condition and needs good rain.
Western Australia looked like having another good season with growers confident of a fairly good crop, Lindsay said.

A range of views formed in the past week on Australia's likely 1997/98 wheat crop, with official forecaster the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) boosting its forecast to 19.2 million tonnes from its earlier projection of 17.8 million tonnes.

This brought ABARE into line with most industry expectations of a crop of around 19 million tonnes. Private forecaster Australian Wheat Forecasters Pty Ltd, however, last week kept its estimate virtually steady on 17.85 million tonnes.

Barley and triticale markets on Australia's east-side formed a focus of domestic grains markets during the week as dairy feed demand grew in dry southern regions, Cameron Pratt of New South Wales grains handling and trading co-operative GrainCo said.
Australian wheat markets dipped this week on expectations of an AWB pools price cut and a reduction in its reserve price in national tenders for wheat from the pools.
Cash wheat fell by A$5.00-A$10.00 a tonne to about A$182.00 Newcastle, while Sydney Futures Exchange (SFE) wheat futures ended virtually steady, on balance, over the week.

Last week featured end-user and merchant buying on the SFE and physical markets, Lindsay said. Other traders said apparent efforts by India and Iraq to re-negotiate wheat import contracts to lower prices had no effect on domestic Australian markets.

Cash sorghum, barley and triticale were all steady over the week, with barley and triticale supported by Victorian dairy demand. Barley ended the week on about A$160.00 a tonne in upcountry NSW, while triticale ended the week on about A$165.00.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
